utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Luckily, the technical problems have been resolved, as we understand. I was informed that there were a few procedural issues to be raised. Mr. Re, you're the first one. I would like to limit at this moment any procedural issue to any matter which has to be dealt with necessarily in relation to this witness at present, not anything else at this moment. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, the Prosecution -- I wish to advise you that after the matters which arose yesterday in court regarding the photo ID boards and whether or not they were shown to the witness, the Prosecution has conducted as thorough a search as it possibly could of all its internal records. We have reviewed our mission reports, all our statements, the photo-boards, investigators' notes. We can find no record of the witness being shown photo-boards which is recorded in the Office of the Prosecutor's system. The searchs are ongoing, but I don't think we're going to find anything. So I'm putting before the Trial Chamber we have done absolutely everything we can to identify what's happened, and it is fairly obvious that had there been some identification process, we surely should have had a record there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're perfectly right, Mr. Re. There should have been. So there are two possibilities: One is that it was never shown to the witness; the other one is that it's not recorded. Of course, that is -- which of the two would be the case is a matter which, of course, concerns the Chamber, the Prosecution, and Defence as well. The parties are instructed -- from our review of the witness list, there might be another source that could provide us with some information and that is a 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There certainly is, but in light of what happened when Your Honours called a surprise witness, so to speak, to the box --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- we had very much limited our inquiries to in-house at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you're instructed also to -- the Chamber has considered the matter. At this moment we'll wait, knowing that one of the witnesses who is on your list, scheduled for, I think, 15 minutes viva voce, who might cast further light on the matter, the Chamber has decided that we'll just wait. And at the same time, when we're talking about proofing, the Chamber instructs all parties not to raise this issue with this witness. Am I clear enough? I'm talking about the 92 bis witness scheduled for 15 minutes. I do not know whether at any stage there will be any protective measures sought in relation to that witness, so therefore I'm not mentioning at this moment his name. But perhaps we could go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Re, any further matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. There was one matter I wished to raise and that was the order Your Honour made -- the Trial Chamber made at the conclusion of the proceedings yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The order is expressed in terms of that particular witness who is -- has the pseudonym Witness 49. The Prosecution, of course, understands the concerns of the Defence and the concerns of the Trial Chamber that resulted in Your Honours making that order in respect of that witness. We, of course, understand that it is very important that there is a record verified by a witness who the Prosecution is speaking to either before court, immediately before court, or during the more -- during the process before of taking a statement which is verified by the witness, so that if there is any issue as to what the witness has said, there is a signed record by the witness and preferably in the witness's own tongue. The Prosecution, in light of the order, which of course we will obey, and in light of the concerns expressed by the Defence and the Trial Chamber, we will not, in respect of any further witnesses, conduct what is being called proofing sessions as such, but anything that a witness says to us which is relevant to the testimony we will reduce to writing and put it into a statement form, and we will have it translated as immediately as we possibly can into the witness's language, whether it's a consolidated statement or a supplement to existing statements, and we will have the witness sign the statement, and we will provide that statement as soon as we possibly can, or the supplement, signed by the witness in his or her own language, with an English -- English language version attached, and if we can get an Albanian one done, we certainly will as well, and we will provide that in the same manner as we were providing proofing notes. So what I'm saying is the Prosecution's approach is the end to proofing notes and we will provide witness statements. There's one other matter in relation to Witness 49. And in case it wasn't clear from when I spoke -- when I addressed the Trial Chamber two days ago and I spoke about what had happened in the days preceding, I was referring to the fact that when Your Honours were asking me about audioing a videolink, we had spoken to him by videolink and it hadn't been audioed. So I was attempting, maybe somewhat obliquely, to convey the message that we had spoken to him. We couldn't correct what had happened in the past, we couldn't go back and record something which had already been said, but we were intending to take a new statement from the witness, which is exactly what we intend to do. We haven't spoken to the witness because the witness, as I am told, arrived here only last night. We intend to try and talk to the witness today sometime and, of course, we'll obey the Court's order to audio-tape any conversation with that witness. Our present plans are to take -- and we have prepared a draft witness statement, based upon what he told us in the past in statements and by videolink. I can't give you the exact date, but I think it was last week. We're planning to provide it all into a consolidated new witness statement. That's one of the reasons why we put the witness -- we're seeking to put the witness down further in the list in an e-mail I sent to the Defence and Trial Chamber last night, and he would be the one, two, three, fourth witness after the next -- fourth witness in line after the next one, which would give the Defence time to prepare with a new witness statement, which we would hope to have signed and translated today; we hope. So if there's any confusion about the way I communicate something, I apologise and I make it quite clear that for transparency, we did talk to him but we did not record it, and we will, of course, record any conversation with this witness and provide any -- provide a witness statement, a new witness statement, consolidated, as quickly as we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, let me try to understand you. You have set out what you're doing at present with the witnesses about to appear, but I'd like to briefly go back to the beginning of your explanation. We have at this moment a request, asking a lot of things, by Mr. Guy-Smith. He wants audio, video, wants it in time -- well, quite a list of things he would like to see. Then we discussed what the position of the Prosecution in this respect was because Mr. Guy-Smith complained that he had not received an answer to his -- not a consolidated answer to his request, and then we were a bit stuck because, in the absence of any answer, we'd have to first resolve the matter for this week, for these days, and then, of course, another matter is whether, in the long term, what finally the Defence would be entitled to receive as far as proofing notes are concerned. Now, we had the list - audio, video -- well, DNA was not yet on that list, but it's a long list, and Mr. Guy-Smith would like to receive a lot of information. What I expected, as a matter of fact, is that you would tell this Chamber that you, in response to what Mr. Guy-Smith said, that you say, Well, this and this and this is what we can offer, and that the Chamber, if there was no agreement between the Defence and Prosecution, would finally decide this matter. From the beginning of your answer, it appears to me - but please correct me if I'm wrong - is that you say, Well, we've decided that we'll make new statements, there will be no recording of proofing sessions. You didn't say that, but you didn't say that there would be recordings. Therefore, this is how we're going to do it, instead of, This is how we respond to the request of the Defence, and since there seems to be still disagreement, we're waiting for the Chamber to make a ruling on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, look, the difficulty is a moment ago, the Trial Chamber said you wanted to confine issues to the witness who was coming in and then you asked -- then you invited me to address you on other issues. I have not been able to provide you with a full answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I tell you why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That is because the issues which have been raised by the Defence, as the Trial Chamber is aware and the Defence are aware, concern all trials in the Tribunal and the practices which are currently and having occurring for a long time. This is a policy decision which has to be made by the management, the Prosecutor herself, and we are in the process of finalising a policy decision. I am offering an interim solution in relation to this trial at the moment in relation to the next witnesses, and saying, In response to Mr. Guy-Smith's and the Defence's request, we will not proof in the sense of what we've been doing in the sense of providing proofing notes, but we will do -- we will provide a witness statement, the same as other witness statements, signed by the Defence which will allow the Defence to, if they need to impeach a witness as to what a witness actually said to the Prosecution because they have a signed version in their hand. That is the Prosecution's position. Now, I note Your Honours issued an order about audio-taping Witness 49. We will do that. If the Trial Chamber is considering expanding the order to other witnesses or other matters, we would like to be fully heard and provide proper -- proper submissions in writing, because there are a number of issues, a number of far-reaching policy and legal issues which must be addressed, and I can't do it in the five to ten minutes, on my feet now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you to do it at this moment. Of course, the Chamber considered the request by Mr. Guy-Smith as the starting point of making further submissions. I think that letter dates already back from six weeks or eight weeks. Therefore -- but let's not deal with the matter at this moment. I just wanted to point out that if you say, This is how we're going to do it, that this Chamber might want to consider whether this Chamber will allow you to do it the way you suggest you do it; that's one. Second, policy decisions made by the Prosecution, fine. Of course, everyone should prepare some policy. But finally this Chamber is responsible for what it considers a fair trial, so if that is well reconciled -- could be reconciled with the policy decisions, then we have no problem; if not, then there might be a problem. We'll spend further time on that, but in the beginning of your answer, you're more or less saying, apart from Witness 49, how you would proceed with the witnesses to come. We'll consider that and see whether that is an acceptable way of dealing with the matter. And then we have, of course, outstanding the long-term matter of how to do it in the whole of the trial, not only the next two weeks or next three weeks, but the whole of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I make it clear that is what the Prosecution is putting on the table, so to speak, in response to the Defence request. The Defence has asked for everything to be audioed, and we're saying we will provide signed written statements from all witnesses. There will be no proofing notes signed by witnesses or proofing notes signed by Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In respect of Witness 49, if proofing notes had been in the process of being prepared, we will disclose today any draft proofing notes, but they will be in the form of a statement anyway so the Defence will get both of them. But that will be later when we've spoken to the witness and that will be audioed. That's our position. We are offering -- we are putting -- our response is signed witness statements translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, my concern is the following, Mr. Re, doing -- after some close reading, you say: "And we are saying we will provide signed witness statements." You're not saying we suggest that instead of following the suggestions made by Mr. Guy-Smith, who didn't only ask for audio, but also for video and a lot of other things, we suggest that we do it this way; you say, We will provide. That suggests that the Prosecution is not making submissions as how to proceed but that the Prosecution is deciding how.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe that's a matter of terminology and the way I'm expressing it. Mr. Guy-Smith has asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't have to go through it again. We'll receive --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we'll receive soon, as I understand, a further response on how to proceed, at least how the OTP would suggest we'd proceed in relation to the matters raised by Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need to put this before the Trial Chamber now because there are other witnesses who will be here on the weekend, and that is this: The Prosecution's suggestion - if that's a better terminology for the Trial Chamber - suggestion is that our intention is to take witness statements, supplementary witness statements, from any witness who comes and to provide them; that is, we take them from the witness, we -- the witness -- in the normal way that you take a witness statement. The witness makes a statement, we ask them questions, and it's put into a witness statement form and the witness signs it in their own language; they have a copy in their own language. That is what we are going to do with any witness who comes over the weekend, absent any order from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider the matter. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I believe there are two issues. The one is the issue of photo identification and the other is the issue of the proofing. I, for the moment, would defer to my colleague Mr. Emmerson with regard to the issue of the proofing since that seems to be the issue which is hot on everybody's mind, because he has been very focused on this issue for the moment, and then I would like for a moment, before I start my examination, to briefly address some issues concerning the photo ident -- concerning the identification issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson, as far as proofing is concerned, let's think about it this weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I was going to say, if I may, that there are lots of larger issues to be discussed, and it is appropriate to seek, discuss, and resolve before the witness who is currently sitting outside this courtroom is dealt with. But there is one matter I ought just to simply raise with Your Honours. Yesterday, after court rose, Your Honours will have received an e-mail from Mr. Oberg containing two sentences setting out an agreed position of understanding between the Prosecution and the Defence, and the contents of that e-mail were specifically agreed by Mr. Guy-Smith and myself and Mr. Re. Later in the evening, I received a communication to indicate that the witness that we're referring to, that is, Witness 49, had already been the subject of a proofing session. That came as some surprise to me, having regard to the comments that are recorded on the transcript, and if I can just give Your Honours the references for the moment, the transcript of Wednesday, the 14th, between pages 118 -- sorry, 1118 and 1125; yesterday's transcript, between 1258 and 1260; and the second sentence, and in particular the words "at all" in the e-mail that Your Honours received from Mr. Oberg yesterday afternoon. I haven't asked Mr. Re at this point, and I'm not asking him whilst this witness is still waiting to come back into court, to provide Your Honours with an explanation, and I will leave it to Your Honours, having considered the transcript, to take whatever measures you think is appropriate. But the fact of the matter is that the witness about whom we had the discussion yesterday afternoon and in respect of whom Mr. Re initially was not prepared to give an undertaking and was then made the subject of an order to tape the proofing session that was upcoming is a witness from whom, it now transpires, a proofing session had already taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give Mr. Re some time to think about a response, and we'll first now continue with the present witness. Mr. Guy-Smith, I do understand that there is a matter you'd like to raise in relation to the photo-spread or the absence of a photo-spread.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. After the journey that we took yesterday, I charted out a variety of different potential conclusions that we could come to with regard to the state of the evidence and realised that we still are in the situation where there is information that we do not have and we may well have as a result of the contemplated witness that we were talking about earlier. Because of that, it is my present intention not to discuss any specific matters, I believe, with this witness concerning any of the issues that I normally would address attendant to the giving of a photo-spread, I think for obvious reasons, since there's information that we just don't have yet. Once we have heard from the investigator, I may need to be in a position to cross-examine the present witness on that issue. That's something that I raised before. I'm not crazy about this; as a matter of fact, I'm really quite reluctant. But I'm reserving, with the Court's indulgence, my right to have any discussion with this particular witness on this issue until we have a clear understanding from all the parties involved as to whether or not it, in fact, occurred. If, in fact, there was no photo-spread ever shown, then I think it raises some very serious issues concerning about the weight of this particular -- this particular witness's - and that's Witness 19's - evidence in many, many regards. But I'm not going to put the cart before the horse with regard to that issue because I think that would be inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The present state of the evidence is that, if I could summarise, that on the basis of the testimony the witness has given, on the basis of what we know - and, of course, we have seen the witness statement - that there is no trace of a positive identification at this moment. Two possibilities: Either it was never tried -- then, of course, you have no positive identification - or it was tried. If it had a result which, let's say, could be considered positive for the Prosecution, then at least it's not recorded. If there was a result which the Prosecution might not consider positive for its case, then it's not recorded either but then there has now been -- there has been no positive identification. So that's where we stand at this moment as far as the evidence is concerned. It could change in five minutes, I don't know, but that's how the Chamber understands at this moment the evidence that has been presented to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am in agreement with that situation. My concern is as follows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith, let's try to keep matters short. I do understand that you are to cross-examine the witness. If the situation which I just briefly described, the situation as far as the evidence, would change in the future, then, of course, you could apply for recalling the witness for further cross-examination. But we expect you to cross-examine the witness as completely as possible at this moment. Of course, if the situation would change at a later stage, then you could ask the Chamber whether an additional opportunity for further cross-examination would be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I firmly intend to. The difficulty -- the difficulty is really with whether or not a particular event occurred, and that's where my difficulty lies. Assume, for purposes of our discussion, Your Honours, that there has been no photo-spread identification, that it never occurred, and you had that information before you right now, that there never was a photo-spread identification of any sense -- excuse me -- of any sense whatsoever. Then my examination of this witness, to be very honest with you, would be very, very different, and the reason for that would be this witness has made a particular number of statements, in that regard detailed statements about an event, which obviously would affect his credibility and his reliability, and it is for that reason that I am concerned about cross-examining this witness in the absence of having the information from the investigator, which I think is the last piece of that particular puzzle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the investigator comes, there are two possibilities: Either he says there was ever a photo-spread shown to the witness or there was not. What -- I mean, if he says it was not, then we have evidence from an interpreter and evidence from the present witness who said there was, at least with -- whether it's a hundred per cent or 95 per cent, or 98 per cent, to what extent, all the details the witness gave are corroborating that there was one. But there are two possibilities: Either the investigator says, Yeah, we've shown that, I mean then it would be even more likely that it has taken place; or he says, It was not, it never took place, then we have conflicting evidence. So you are seeking a solution for a situation that it is established that there never was. That is a situation which is not likely to occur unless the investigator would say, There never was, and then the witness says, Oh, no, no, all the details, all about the photo-spread, that's -- well, it was all a great mistake or ... Therefore, we want you to cross-examine the witness as completely as possible under the present circumstances, which I briefly described.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. I will follow the Chamber's direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any other matter? I don't think so. Then we would like the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Usher, would you -- Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just whilst he's being brought in, would Your Honour have it in mind to return to the question of the recording of proofing sessions at some point during the day since there's likely to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least for the weekend. At least for the weekend, you need a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's first -- at a later moment today. But I'll take the opportunity to discuss the matters during the break with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 19, you're at quite distance at this moment. Witness 19, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Guy-Smith, counsel for Mr. Balaj. Mr. Guy-Smith, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, we're in a microphone on, microphone off situation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good. I just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm going to be asking you a series of questions this morning. In the event that you have any difficulty understanding any of the questions that I ask you, please let me know. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to start with talking to you about the statements that you have made to various investigators during this case, okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The first time that you made a statement to the investigators was in 2004. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you made the statement to the investigators, that statement was read back to you by an interpreter. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after the statement was read back to you by an interpreter, you signed the statement, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, dealing with the first statement, just the first statement, when you were signing the statement, do you remember that you signed each and every page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I do know that I signed every statement that I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The very first statement that you made, did you have any difficulty understanding the statement that was read back to you by the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every statement that I gave was read entirely, just to check if there was any mistake. If there was any minor mistake, then we would correct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Did you get a chance in the first statement, as you sit here today, do you remember correcting any mistakes that you found in the first statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the second statement, the second statement you made that you signed, that happened, I believe, in the year 2005. Do you recall that? I think you said you recalled making each and every one of them, but I just want to be sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I gave a statement in 2004 and in 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, it's a bit confusing, of course, on the basis of the paper we have. We have two interviews in 2004, so -- although it's put in one paper. Could you please clarify that with the witness as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In 2004, do you recall meeting with the investigators on two separate occasions; once, I believe, in July and once in October?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You signed the statement after you met him the second time in October; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I signed every statement that I gave, regardless of whether it was in 2004 or 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to the statement that you made in 2005, do you recall making any corrections in that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember making corrections to this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After that, after 2005, you made another statement and that was in 2006. And if it might help refresh your recollection, that was a statement that you made with an investigator who was a woman who spoke French. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, I take it your answer would be the same. The statement was translated for you, you listened to it, you had the opportunity to make any corrections, there were no corrections to be made, and you signed it; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you are not fully reflecting the earlier evidence of the witness. You, in your question, assumed that there were no corrections, where the witness testified several times that he doesn't remember whether he made any corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please be precise in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Most definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall in 2006, when you made the statement with the investigator who spoke French to you, whether you made any corrections to the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave the statement. If there was any correction, we made it. Then we read it in Albanian. Then she asked if the statement was okay, and I said it was okay, and then she asked me if I had any remarks, and I said I didn't have any remarked, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Each and every time that you made a statement, that being in 2004, 2005, and 2006, a statement that you signed, you did not sign that statement before you were satisfied that it was a correct statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would like, with the Court's permission, for the usher to give the witness a piece of paper and a pen so that he can sign his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, do we have a piece of paper and a pen? Perhaps it would even be good to have that on the ELMO, to the extent possible, so that we can see and follow what the witness actually does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to write my full name or my signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could first write your full name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Shouldn't we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that we should go into private session for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall there being a headquarters at a former grocery shop in Ratis? Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, I did not visit a shop in Ratis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So your answer would be no, then? That's something that is not in your memory, that there was a former grocery shop of Zef Avdyli which was the headquarters, a place where people would go to get authorisation to travel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you've told us that you -- I'm sorry. Did you ever get any authorisations to travel outside of your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me personally, but members of my family, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, your microphone is open, and I don't think that your conversations with staff should be on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm just double-checking. I appreciate that. Could we please have 2D21-0253, and that would be paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you've just told us that you never personally went to get authorisation to travel outside of your village; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have a need to travel and we did get travel authorisation, but I personally didn't go to get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall telling the investigator in this very first statement that you made with regard to your recognition of an identification of Idriz Balaj, as Toger, the following: "As it comes to Idriz Balaj, a.k.a. Toger, I'm certain it was him because I've seen him many times, when I had to go to the headquarters to get authorisations to travel and so." Do you recall making that statement to the investigators, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall this statement. I did go with my sister or with my brother when I need -- we needed to get this travel authorisation. But I didn't go inside the building, I waited outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I take it the statement that you made just a moment ago, which is, "We did have a need to travel and we did get travel authorisation but I didn't personally -- but I personally didn't go to get it" is not true? You went to get travel authorisation is what you've just told us. A moment ago, you told us you did not go to get personal -- to get travel authorisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't go to get the document. I went to that place with my brother or with my sister, but I stayed outside, I didn't go inside. I was very young. I was scared. I just stayed outside while a member of my family would go inside to get the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the statement in 2004 you weren't scared, were you? And you used this, and by "this," I mean you're travelling to get authorisation as a basis, as a foundation, for your identification of Idriz Balaj as Toger? Isn't that what you did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is that I saw him while the headquarters was there, but I didn't say that I went to that place personally to get a travel authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was the information that I read to you in your statement, then, incorrect, when you said "I'm certain it was him because I've seen him many times when I had to go to the headquarters to get authorisations to travel"? When you made that statement to the investigator, was that a lie? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I object to this line of questioning. There hasn't been any establishment as to what happened when this witness went to the -- to the headquarters. He's told the Trial Chamber that he went there, waited outside while his brothers or sisters attended to business. Now, that does not preclude the possibility of making identifications based on those visits, for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that -- MR. DI FAZIO: Therefore, to be putting to the witness that what he said is inconsistent with what he's now telling you -- what he said in his statement is now inconsistent with what he's telling you is unfair, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think it's absolutely fair, Your Honour, precisely for the reasons of what is contained in the language that we have here in the statement. But I'm happy -- I'm happy to leave it alone any further. I think the point has been made. The reason that he claims to have identified my client is based upon a particular act that he engaged in. That was to go get authorisations, which he personally did and he did it many times. I don't think the question is unfair at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the idea, or the point from the witness side, if he went to these headquarters, if he was there, present, he had the opportunity to observe, if that was -- if that's what he said he was doing. There isn't necessarily a contradiction between that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll continue -- I'll continue with your thought in mind, but I view the evidence in a slightly different fashion. But if that's the way the Chamber is viewing it, I'm happy to do it in -- I'm happy to proceed along the lines which I believe the Chamber is concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you earlier said that you could move on because the point was clear. Whatever the point is, it is clear, so you're invited to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take some comfort in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In early March, did you see KLA members in your village, people wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What year do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them sometimes, but when problems started for my family, then I began to see them more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of anyone else apart from Rexhepi, Islami and Zefi that you claim to have seen during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall them for the moment. I couldn't recall the names of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: These men, as you've told us, would drive up and down the road in your village; is that correct? And this is in 1998, before the trouble started with your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them, but I saw also others whom I didn't know, just driving past in their cars or walking. But I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were, as you've said, young. How old were you in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirteen. Thirteen or 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for a moment, I'm concerned about ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your eldest brother at the time, in 1998, he was in prison, was he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from the eldest sister, the rest of the family, meaning yourself and your other brothers and sisters, were too young to join any forces, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to talk to you about some other people who I believe lived in your village or close to your village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And we may need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the issue of in which way proofing sessions, that is, conversations with witnesses in preparation of the testimony, in which way they should be recorded and to what extent recordings should be disclosed to the other party. This discussion started by way of correspondence between the parties. The responses were not consolidated responses. There was some disagreement on when to respond and when the other party should respond. We now find ourselves in a situation where the Prosecution is considering policy decisions, et cetera. The Chamber considers the matter important enough to make it an issue in this trial and not just correspondence and policies. So, therefore, the parties are invited to make submissions on the matter so that we can come to a decision, a long-term decision. That will take some time. Mr. Re has asked for guidance for this weekend. The Prosecution is ordered to audio-record the conversations, proofing sessions, whatever you call them, sessions in preparing of new statements, well, whatever, but conversations with witnesses who arrived and are preparing for their testimony. This order does not include that this audio-recording should be disclosed to the Defence. That's another matter. We'll wait and see whether there's any reason to consider at a later stage whether it would be fair for the Defence to rely upon information from these audio-recordings. So the order is limited to the recording itself so that the recording does exist. And the parties are invited -- may I ask you, Mr. Re and Defence counsel, what would you consider a reasonable time to make any written submissions on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From the Prosecution's -- it's now Friday. From our view, I would suggest Wednesday is realistic for us to get a proper, full written submission surveying the law and all policy issues in as comprehensive a format as we possibly could to be of the greatest assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Defence. Could they agree on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm perfectly happy to agree on Wednesday. I don't know whether Your Honour would wish to have sequential submissions or simultaneous submissions. I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands as to which would be more useful; in other words, whether you would like to hear the Prosecution's position and then for the Defence to respond or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think, as a matter of fact, the discussion had started already. The positions are to some extent known, so we'd like to have simultaneous submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any need at a later stage to hear further from you then --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very happy to do that, and we will endeavour to collaborate between the three Defence parties so that you have one submission from the Defence rather than three. Can I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for your clarification, the issue the Chamber does not seek to include at this moment is whether proofing sessions are permissible, yes or no. We know that there's an ICC decision; the Chamber is aware of the decision. We have two decisions in this Tribunal which take a different route compared to the ICC. That's not at this moment what we are seeking. We're just seeking about recording and disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Entirely understood. Can I just seek two points of clarification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all, we understand Your Honours to have to directed the Prosecution to make recordings, or they're not to disclose them until this matter is resolved, is that correct, not simply over the weekend but until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said over the weekend, but then, of course, we'll consider that. But the most urgent thing first was to see what would happen over the weekend, and it might well be that we extend that on from Monday, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Does Your Honour, at some stage - and again I'm not pressing for it to be dealt with now - wish to return to the issue of the witness in respect of whom the order was made yesterday evening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm entirely in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not off our mind. There are a few other matters of the last week that might need further attention as well. We might consider them also in -- but at this moment, it's not an issue we'd like to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, then, the Chamber expects both parties to file submissions by Friday -- by Wednesday next week. Then there's another matter raised which has some -- that's the issue of what should be pleaded. First of all, Mr. Guy-Smith, the Chamber does allow you to cautiously, also in view of age and -- to put questions to the witness you started doing, but there is a more fundamental issue involved there as well, and the -- what should have been pleaded and what should not have been pleaded is a legal matter on which the Chamber also would like to receive submissions if the Prosecution insists on its -- on the objection raised. Mr. Di Fazio raised the objection. If he says, Well, I don't need to further insist on excluding testimony to be heard when this defence is not pleaded - it's not one of the special defences, as we know them from the Rules - if the Prosecution insists, then we'd like to receive written submissions on the matter, and those would be sequential submissions because then the Defence will be in a position to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution does insist. The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- is really surprised that Mr. Emmerson, after filing a pre-trial brief, in which he took issue with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Re -- Mr. Re, you have full opportunity to make whatever submissions you want. It was just to say that if you do not want to pursue the matter, the Chamber does not require you to make submissions. If you do want to pursue the matter, then the Chamber would like to receive submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We will and we'll be seeking an order from the Trial Chamber in relation to the Defence. That will be in our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I invite the Prosecution on the record to make it clear in their written argument so that the Defence can respond to it whether the suggestion is being advanced that lack of pleading of a matter to be raised in cross-examination should result in the exclusion or prevention of the cross-examination or merely be the subject of comment at the conclusion of the proceedings, bearing in mind that the rules on special defences do not, specifically do not, prevent the evidence being led but merely allow the Trial Chamber to draw inferences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this suggestion, Mr. Re, I don't ask you to respond right away. You'll consider it when preparing your submissions. When could we expect these submissions? I'm not pushing to have this resolved in one or two days. I mean, it's a fundamental issue, as Mr. Emmerson said. Would a week do?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think a week would be realistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If we have any difficulty, I'll let the Trial Chamber know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And would the Defence oppose -- a week means Friday next week. If Mr. Re would like to work over the weekend to finalise it and make it even better, would Monday be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perfectly acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you have -- now I have to think about what day that is. The 19th? No, next Monday is the 19th. That would be the 26th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's correct, but the Monday, week, would be better than Friday, week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A little bit over a week, yes. Okay, that's ... Madam Registrar confirms that it's the 26th of March. Then, Mr. Guy-Smith, are you ready to continue your cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the witness is -- the usher is invited to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, on all the matters where we will receive submissions, it goes without saying, of course, that we'd very much like to have legal authorities cited but also reference to tradition and practice in courts, whether international courts or domestic courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to your last ruling, do we take it that's in relation to both submissions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that the first one, certainly on proofing sessions, needs reference to domestic and international practice, and as I told you already that the Chamber is aware of the ICC decision. And, of course, the second one is of a similar legal nature where we'd like to be informed as fully as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, when you continue, of course, you are requested also to consider to what extent the issues you'd like to raise are necessarily -- necessarily be elicited from this witness or by any other written sources, if they do exist. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm waiting for the curtains to go up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- I think we -- did we deal with the matter in private session? Then we should have redaction and we should return into private session now, when we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed after it's confirmed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to discuss with you now your testimony concerning your claims that you saw Toger with your sister, sister S. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've testified that you saw a person that you have named Toger bring your sister to the family home after she had been gone for about a week; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That he was in the presence of some other soldiers; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That you were present in, I believe it was, the yard when that happened; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to that testimony, there's not a doubt in your mind that you were present, and you saw Toger bring sister S to the house; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him with my own eyes when he brought her, and I was there for the entire duration of the visit. This is -- I'm certain about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 2D21-243, and that would be paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Guy-Smith, that we have not yet assigned a number to the previous. Would that -- is that a different statement or is it the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. So if we could -- I apologise. And if we could assign a number to the previous statement, whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was the statement ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2004. And now you're referring to this one, as the 2005?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2006. Okay, that's clear. Madam Registrar, the 2004 statement, July/October, would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit number D9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification at this moment. Then the -- may I take it that the 2006 statement would then be D10?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Also marked for identification, both under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall telling the investigator, that is, the French woman that you spoke to in 2006 with regard to your sister, that sister S coming to the house to visit, the following: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The statement goes on, but with regard to what I'm discussing with you at this point, I'm not going to continue with that paragraph. Do you remember making that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember saying this and I also remember that that day, when she came, I was not there, but later on when I went home I found her there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We need a redaction, and I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A redaction will be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So your testimony, as you sit here today, is that you were not there when she came; correct? You did not see her come to the house; correct? You saw her later; she was already at the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Therefore, the information that you gave us yesterday, that you saw her come to the house with Toger, was not true, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they came to take her away, it was Toger and two other soldiers who came.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, that's not the question I asked you, and I would like an answer to my question. When you told this Chamber yesterday that you were at the house and you saw her arrive and you saw her arrive in the presence of Toger, when you made that statement yesterday to this Chamber, you were not telling the truth, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first visit, when she came the first time for a visit, she was brought by Toger who was in company of two other soldiers, and this is what I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You didn't see Toger bring your sister to the house. You just told us that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, were you not speaking of the second visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, there were two visits; the first one and one that happened later. Now I'm speaking about the first one, and this is what I saw with my own eyes. It was a jeep, there were two or three other soldiers, and it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... during the second visit, you did not see Toger bring her to the house, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, before we continue, in order for the Chamber to follow this testimony and follow the line of questioning, I would very much like you to draw our attention to the relevant pages so that we can also see in which -- from which context you are quoting and look at it, because if there would be any possible confusion about the first or the second visit, then we'd like to identify that as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely, Your Honour. I'm using --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 15th of March, you said yesterday, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The 15th of March. I'm using the unofficial transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give a word which is not found on every line, then it's very easy for us to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "White Niva car."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: White Niva car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be the answer. The question was, yesterday: "All right. Thank you. Now let's focus your attention on the second visit when your sister come back. Again, how did she arrive at -- how did she make her way to your house?" Answer: "She was brought by Toger and two soldiers for a visit and they were in Niva, a white Niva car."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request for the counsel to wait for the interpretation to finish before he poses his question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you testified to that yesterday, that wasn't true, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please explain what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. You were asked a question by the Prosecution yesterday concerning the second visit of your sister, sister S, to the house. At that time you were asked the following question and you gave the following response: "Q. All right. Thank you. Now, let's focus your attention on the second visit when your sister came back again. Again, how did she arrive at -- how did she make her way to your house?" And your answer, sir, was as follows: "A. She was brought by Toger and two soldiers for a visit. They were in a Niva, a white Niva car."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I've listened to your previous question which relates to the same and you are suggesting that there is an unambiguous contradiction. I have great difficulties in following that; therefore, I would like you to put the question in such a way to the witness that it's not suggesting what you suggested earlier in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've just told us here in court, but a few moments ago, that you saw Toger bring your sister on the second visit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, my sister had said that she was brought there by Toger and two or three other soldiers, that she arrived at home, but on that day, I saw Toger when he came with two or three other soldiers in a white Niva, only with a windscreen. To my recollection, I know that I saw my sister that day, that we spent together some time, three or four hours, and I also know that she set off in the direction of the place where she was supposed to return, and I also know that shortly after, Toger came with one or two other soldiers --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you should wait until the translation has been finished, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Don't interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say in the answer that you've just given us, did you also know that shortly after -- I'm sorry. When you say that you know that Toger came with one or two soldiers, is that -- are you telling us now that that is information that you received from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that I saw with my own eyes. I'm not speaking of things that I heard. I'm just speaking of things that I saw with my own eyes that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So there's no confusion, on the second visit, when sister S, your sister S, came to the home, did you see a white car drive up; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, to my recollection, I was just a small distance away from the house. I was involved in work or something, and then shortly after, I returned home and I found my sister there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll ask you the same question again, sir, and I'll ask you, please, to give me an answer yes or no. So there's no confusion, on the second visit, when your sister, your sister S, came to the home, did you see a white car drive up; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, we are not going to proceed on this way because there's a lot of confusion created. I will put one or two questions to the witness. Witness 19, you told us that you did not see with your own eyes at the second visit that your sister was brought to your home but you found her when you returned to home, already there. At the same time, you tell us that you saw a white Niva car with Toger. Did you intend to say that you saw Toger in the white Niva car on that same day when your sister came home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the second visit, I saw what you described on the same day, a white Niva, on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Toger in that white Niva; is that correctly understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, where did you see, on that same day, the white Niva with Toger in it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was near the house when the Niva approached the yard of the house and when he asked where my sister was, because the time has come for her to return, and we told him that she had set off with one of our brothers to the direction of the place where she was supposed to return. And then they left immediately after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There were two separate occasions on the second visit when you saw a white Niva; correct? One was in the morning when your sister came and one was in the afternoon after your sister had left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first day, in the morning, I know that I saw him very far from the house. I was not in the house; I was far from the house. A few minutes later, when I returned home, I found my sister there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because we now have the answer of the first day, I'm going to, once again, seek to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not perfectly clear to me that -- the witness said, "On the first day ..." In your last answer, Witness, when you said, "On the first day, in the morning, I know that I saw him very far from the house. He was not in the house." Was that the first visit where your sister was all the time accompanied by those who brought her or was this at the second visit where they left her with you, with the family, for some time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about the second visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say at the second visit, did you -- when you were not at home when your sister arrived, did you nevertheless see the white Niva car from a distance? Is that how I should understand your testimony? And I'm talking about approximately the time of the arrival, not the moment where they were coming to fetch her and she had left already, but upon arrival. Did you, when you were not at home, see from a distance the white Niva car then or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw from a distance of 50, 60 metres, I saw that white car, but it never occurred to me that it would headed towards our house. But when my sister got out of the car, it drove off immediately, and then I returned home after a while and found the sister there, and we stayed for -- together for -- all of us, for three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you saw the car coming to the house, how many people were in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, in the morning, I can't remember how many people there were because it was quite a distance away from the place I was sitting. I'm talking of the morning visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the witness now corrected you in identifying whether it was the car arriving in the morning or the afternoon. That should have been clear in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What were they wearing when you saw them from a distance of 50 to 60 metres in the morning visit as they were driving in a white car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not easy for me to ascertain what they were wearing. That day, in the afternoon, I could see clearly who they were and what they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm only talking about the morning now. In the morning, could you tell what the people -- I'm sorry. In the morning, when you saw the white car come on the second visit, could you tell what else was in that white car? And by that I mean, apart from people, could you see weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the white car but couldn't see weapons or anything because it -- the car stopped for a very brief moment, maybe a minute, and then I didn't see it anymore. And I couldn't recognise the persons who were in that car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us, as you sit here today, approximately how long a period of time passed from when you first saw the white car from a distance of 50 to 60 metres in the morning when your sister, sister S, came to visit until it disappeared from your sight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very brief time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was it 10 or 15 seconds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 30 seconds up to 1 minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Your sister remained with you for some hours that day and then she left; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When she left --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've told us -- you told us, I believe, yesterday that during the first visit of your sister, you invited Toger in for coffee; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. During the first visit, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That he came in and spent some time with the family drinking coffee; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: True. This is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: About how long did he spend drinking coffee with your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember right, 20 or 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did he sit down in a chair at a table?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near the house, in the field outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did all of the participants in the coffee-drinking do that outside of the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was hot weather and inside it was hot. This happens when it's cold weather. But at the time -- at that time it was hot, and we were sitting in the shade near the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that you spent a short time with Toger and two other soldiers taking a refreshment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that is on page -- it would be on pages 4 and 5, will be the general subject matter, of yesterday's proceedings. That's on the unofficial transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you to say it right from the beginning. I found it on pages 4 and 5. I thought I'd find it easily by searching for coffee. There's no "coffee" in there. Refreshments, drinks? Would you please be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked the following question and you gave the following answer, and it's where it says: "We invited him in. We offered something to drink to him." When you invited him in, did you invite him into your house and did you have coffee -- excuse me, did you have a drink in the house or was that in the garden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first visit, whatever we offered them as refreshments was done so outside. Not inside the house but in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. During that time, did you see a scar on his mouth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment I was talking with my sister, and I didn't look carefully at his face or at whatever you are putting to me, because the visit lasted very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have told us that one of the ways that you recognised this man you've called Toger was that he had a scar over his right lip; correct? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, that's not strictly true. What he said was, I recognise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not discuss it. Mr. Guy-Smith, please, the line where we find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. It's in response to the question of "unusual features" on page 53 of yesterday's transcript. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no doubt of that. I have no doubt of that. What I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked for it so that I can read it, and then we can see what ... I'm just trying to find out, 53, in which visit we are there at that moment, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This would be -- this would be neither visit, Your Honour. This, as a matter of fact, would be with regard to a night-time incident concerning another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So my question really is had he seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll now re-read your question so that we know exactly whether that -- because that was the concern, that what was put to the witness was not reflecting properly the testimony. Is that it? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, essentially yes, because the question implied that there was a scar, was the method by which recognition occurred, took place. That wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Guy-Smith will literally put to the witness, I take it, what he said and then formulate his question. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, eventually I will do that, but I think this is a legitimate way of testing -- could we have the headphones off for a minute, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since there were specific questions posed by the Prosecution yesterday with regard to any unusual features --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- on Toger's face, it seems to me to be fair questioning to ask this witness whether or not he saw that scar at any other time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not, I think, what your question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And also -- and also, whether or not the scar itself, because that was the thrust of the questioning that was being done by Mr. Di Fazio yesterday, whether the scar itself was one of the bases upon which this particular witness was able to recognise the individual known as Toger. MR. DI FAZIO: And it's that second assertion that I take issue with, it's the second assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that case, I'll -- in that case, I'll proceed with questioning to clarify the first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The first issue is fine; the second is not permissible. Please proceed. Could the witness put his earphones up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You claim to have seen a scar on the face of the individual you have identified as Toger; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but this has to do with another occasion. I mentioned this in another context.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. The scar that you saw, you saw late at night; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It was in your home, and you claim that you saw it as a result of flashlights being shone upon the person's face; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, how long a period of time did you have when you saw the person that night? How long were you looking at their face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, probably for 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's your testimony that when your sister, that's sister M, was taken, that the people who came to the house were there for 15 or 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. This is what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during the time that you were involved in the second incident, when your sister, sister M, was taken, were you in the presence of the individual who you saw, who had a scar on his face, the whole time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The scar that you saw on this individual's face? Was it a big scar? Was it a long scar? Could you describe it for the Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the upper lip. It was neither very big nor small. Kind of average, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say it was kind of average, could you give us a length of the scar? Was it -- and I'm, for the record --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately so big.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the witness has put his thumb and forefinger out, and I would say approximately -- I'm always very bad at this, but I may have a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite the witness to point again? I would say one to one and a half centimetres would be, even from this distance. Mr. Emmerson, you are closer. Would you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It looked like about 1.5 centimetres, longer than a centimetre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A little bit longer than a centimetre. Please proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this scar that you saw, it was an old scar; correct? Something that had been around for a while?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a tattoo sign. It looked like an old scar, like, you know, what remains after an accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was it a slightly different colour than the rest of the skin on his -- on his upper lip?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't look at the colour. I do know that there was a scar on the upper lip, and I can't tell you anything about the colour. If you understand what a scar is, this is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
